analysis.one_liner: Ends tax breaks, royalty relief, and liability caps for fossil-fuel companies.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate in April 2015, referred to the Finance Committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strip away a long list of federal supports for coal, oil, and natural gas companies: about a dozen tax preferences, the government's ability to waive royalty payments on offshore oil and gas leases, a liability cap on companies responsible for oil spills, and federal loans and financing that support fossil-fuel projects at home and abroad. It would also raise the minimum royalty rate companies pay on federal coal, oil, and gas leases, add a 13% tax on Gulf of Mexico offshore oil and gas, and increase the per-barrel fee that funds oil-spill cleanup.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently fund roughly $70+ billion in fossil-fuel subsidies that would be redirected to the Treasury; coastal communities and anyone harmed by oil spills, who would no longer face a cap on what a responsible company owes; and federal treasuries in energy-producing states, which would collect higher royalties on coal, oil, and gas taken from public land.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals royalty relief authority so oil and gas companies pay full royalties on offshore leases instead of having them waived.
Raises the minimum royalty rate on federal coal, oil, and gas leases from 12.5% to 18.75% of the value extracted.
Removes the limit on how much companies must pay for offshore oil-spill damages, so taxpayers are not left covering costs beyond $75 million plus related cleanup.

Terminates more than a dozen tax preferences for fossil-fuel companies, including percentage depletion, intangible drilling cost expensing, the domestic manufacturing deduction for oil, gas, and coal income, and the corporate tax exemption for publicly traded fossil-fuel partnerships.

Stops federal financing of fossil-fuel projects through the World Bank, the Export-Import Bank, the Overseas Private Investment Corporation, the Rural Electrification Administration, and Department of Transportation rail and port grants.
Adds a 13% tax on Gulf of Mexico offshore oil and gas production and raises the per-barrel fee that finances oil-spill response from 8 to 10 cents.

analysis.who_pays: Coal, oil, and natural gas companies, which would lose several billion dollars a year in tax breaks, higher royalties, and cheaper federal financing; electric utility ratepayers and fuel consumers could see modest price increases as some of these costs are passed through.

drawbacks.text: Ending tax preferences and raising royalties on domestic producers would raise production costs, and some of those costs could be passed to consumers through higher fuel and electricity prices.

The bill directs federal agencies and lenders to stop supporting fossil-fuel projects, which would cut off financing options for coal-reliant communities and rural electric cooperatives that currently use these programs.
The bill as written was never scored in committee, so its exact effect on federal revenue, energy prices, and jobs was never tested in a hearing or markup.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's central claim — that profitable fossil-fuel companies should not receive federal support — is a straightforward trade: it would raise revenue and reduce pollution risk, at the cost of higher production costs for coal, oil, and gas companies that would likely be partly passed to energy consumers. Its weakness is political feasibility and the fact that some of its costs would land on communities dependent on those industries, and it was never refined through the normal committee process.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Finance Committee in April 2015, and the committee took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the two-year Congress.

narrative.text: Sen. Sanders introduced the bill on April 22, 2015.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day.
That referral was the bill's last action; the Finance Committee never scheduled a hearing or markup, and the Senate never voted on it before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
The bill's own findings note that oil, gas, coal, utility, and mining industries spent more than $1.8 billion on lobbying between 2010 and 2014 to protect tax loopholes and subsidies.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal, oil, and natural gas companies kept every federal subsidy, tax preference, royalty break, and liability cap the bill targeted, and the industries that lobbied to keep those provisions paid nothing.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to end fossil-fuel subsidies, royalty relief, and oil-spill liability caps.

for.name: 2 of 44 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other senators joined.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican majority
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred; the bill received no further action in either chamber.

against.name: Fossil-fuel and utility lobbying interests
against.role: Industries whose subsidies the bill targeted
against.what_they_did: Spent more than $1.8 billion on lobbying during 2010-2014 to preserve the tax loopholes and subsidies this bill would have eliminated.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor is an independent who caucuses with Democrats and it drew only 2 Democratic cosponsors with no Republican support, and it died in a committee controlled by a Republican majority without a vote.

industries.note: The bill repeals their royalty relief on offshore leases, raises the federal royalty rate they pay, ends about a dozen tax preferences including intangible drilling cost expensing and percentage depletion, imposes a 13% Gulf of Mexico severance tax, and lifts the cap on their oil-spill liability — all costs that currently come out of taxpayer pockets or spill victims' hands.
The bill raises the federal coal royalty rate from 12.5% to 18.75%, repeals percentage depletion and other coal tax preferences, and directs federal programs to stop financing coal projects.
The bill repeals the corporate income tax exemption these partnerships use to avoid entity-level taxation on fossil-fuel income, a structure unique to oil, gas, and coal businesses.

industries.industry: International lenders and export credit agencies (World Bank, Export-Import Bank, OPIC)
industries.note: The bill rescinds unobligated funds and prohibits future use of U.S. money at these agencies to finance fossil-fuel power plants and projects abroad, with a narrow exception for Least Developed Countries.

industries.industry: Rural electric cooperatives and federal fossil-energy research programs
industries.note: The bill terminates the Energy Department's Office of Fossil Energy Research and Development and bars Rural Electrification Administration loans for fossil-fuel projects, ending programs that some rural communities and fossil-energy researchers rely on.
